title: What Is a Put Option?
subtitle: The right to sell an asset at a fixed price - expecting a price drop or wanting to insure a portfolio
openingQuestion: You hold stock Y at a price of VND 100,000, worried it might fall. How does buying a put option with a strike of VND 95,000 help?
openingOptions: It only helps if the price rises
If the price falls below VND 95,000, you still have the right to sell at 95,000 - capping your maximum loss, like buying insurance for your portfolio
You are forced to sell the stock immediately
explanation: A put option gives the right to sell an asset at a predetermined price, so its value rises when the market falls. Its most common application isn't speculation but insurance: someone holding a stock buys a put option to lock in a floor price for their position. The right way to think about the fee is also like an insurance premium - you pay a certain amount to eliminate an uncertain, but potentially very large, loss.

diagram.label: Buy a Put Option at the strike price
Market price falls below the strike
Still sell at the higher strike price

realWorldExample.description: Large pension funds often buy put options on the S&P 500 index to protect their portfolio from sudden sharp declines, accepting the premium paid as a recurring insurance-like cost.

quiz.question: What position is the seller (writer) of a put option in?
options: An obligation to buy at the strike if the buyer exercises - receiving the premium
A right to choose whether to exercise or not, exactly like the put buyer
No risk at all, since they already received the premium upfront
Always required to sell the asset before the option expires
quiz.explanation: This is the asymmetry of rights in every option: the BUYER has a right (no obligation), the SELLER (writer) always has an OBLIGATION if the buyer exercises. In exchange, the writer receives the premium.

quiz.question: An investor holding a stock sells (writes) a covered call on that same stock (committing to sell at the strike if the buyer exercises). What does this strategy cap, and where does its income come from?
options: A covered call is always riskier than simply holding the stock ordinarily
This strategy only benefits when the stock price falls sharply and quickly
It caps nothing and generates no additional income at all
It caps upside gain in exchange for premium income
quiz.explanation: A covered call is a popular "income generation" strategy: the investor accepts capping their upside gain in exchange for certain premium income.

quiz.question: Why does an investor holding a stock buy a put option?
options: To set a floor on the sale price, capping the possible loss
To increase profit if the stock continues to rise sharply
To receive additional premium income from a put seller
To drop the obligation to hold the stock until expiration
quiz.explanation: This is a protective put - true portfolio insurance. However far the stock falls, it can still be sold at the strike, in exchange for the premium forfeited if the price doesn't fall.

quiz.question: Buying a put at a strike of VND 40,000, premium VND 2,000. Price at expiration is VND 33,000. What is the net gain?
options: VND 7,000 (= 40,000 − 33,000, forgetting to subtract the premium)
VND 2,000 (exactly equal to the premium spent upfront)
VND 9,000 (= 40,000 − 33,000 + 2,000, adding the premium)
quiz.explanation: The intrinsic value at expiration is VND 7,000, minus the VND 2,000 premium leaves a net gain of VND 5,000. A put's break-even point is the strike minus the premium, here VND 38,000.

quiz.question: What risk does a put seller take on?
options: Being forced to sell stock at the strike even though the market price has risen
Being forced to buy stock at the strike even though the market price has fallen sharply
Losing the entire premium received if the stock price stays flat
No risk at all, since the premium was already received
quiz.explanation: Selling a put is a commitment to buy in at the strike no matter how far the price falls. The risk is bounded - the lowest price is zero - but the maximum loss can still be nearly the entire strike value.

keyTakeaways: Put option: the right to sell at the strike price, profitable when price falls
Protective put: the most common portfolio insurance strategy
The seller of an option has an obligation, the buyer only has a right - an asymmetric risk

practicePrompt.question: You are holding VNM stock and worried the price could fall sharply soon, so you buy an option that lets you sell this stock at a fixed price of VND 90,000, no matter how far the market price falls. Which type of option lets you 'insure' your investment this way?
options: Put option: the right to sell at the strike price, profitable when price falls
Call option: the right to buy at the strike price, profitable when price rises
A Forward, because this is a binding contract to sell the stock at a fixed price
There is no derivative instrument that can protect an investment from downside price risk
practicePrompt.explanation: Put option: the right to sell at the strike price, profitable when price falls. This is a common hedging tool (protective put) - an investor holding a stock buys a put option to cap downside risk, like buying insurance for a portfolio.

sections.text: A put option gives the right to SELL an asset at a predetermined strike price - a tool for someone who expects the price to fall, or who simply wants to insure a held asset against downside risk.

The most common strategy with a put option is the protective put: an investor holding an asset buys an additional put option to cap downside risk. If the price falls sharply, they still have the right to sell at the chosen strike, instead of suffering an uncapped loss following the market's decline. Large pension funds often buy put options on the S&P 500 index to protect their portfolio from sudden sharp declines, accepting the premium paid as a recurring insurance-like cost.
The put seller: an obligation, not a right

The seller (writer) of a put option has an obligation to BUY the asset at the strike price if the put buyer decides to exercise their right - in exchange, they receive the premium upfront as income, regardless of whether the right is later exercised. This is the core asymmetry of every option: the buyer has a choice, the seller always has an obligation.
Covered call: turning a held stock into an income source

A related strategy is the covered call: an investor holding a stock sells (writes) a call option on that same stock, committing to sell at the strike if the right is exercised. In exchange for immediate premium income, they accept a cap on maximum gain - if price rises above the strike, they must still sell at the strike, missing out on the extra upside. Suits an investor expecting the price to move sideways or rise only slightly.

items: Put option: the right to SELL at the strike price, profitable when price falls
Protective put: buying a put to insure a held asset
Covered call: selling a call on a held stock to generate income, in exchange for a cap on upside
The option seller always has an obligation if the buyer exercises the right
